definition: A fable is a short, openly invented tale that teaches a lesson — often through talking animals — and, by extension, any account that is invention rather than fact.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandfather passed it off as family history, but the tale of the wolf who guarded our orchard is pure fable — no wolf, no orchard, just a lesson about patience he wanted us to keep.
An anecdote is milder stuff than a fable: one small moment offered as true, nothing invented and nothing to prove — a fable invents freely and aims its whole tale at a single lesson.
Myth goes further than fable: a fable spends its invention on one compact lesson, while a myth swells to carry a people's entire picture of the world — origins, gods, and all.

A parable teaches through lifelike, everyday people — two debtors, a lost sheep, a quarrel over a well — events that could happen on any street. A fable announces its invention from the first line: talking beasts, impossible bargains, a tale nobody was ever meant to believe.

A yarn is a long, colorful story spun mainly for the fun of the telling, and it sprawls wherever the teller wanders. A fable is compact and aimed: every invented detail exists to deliver the one lesson waiting at the end.

A fable is a short, openly invented tale that teaches a lesson — often through talking animals — and, by extension, any account that is invention rather than fact.
In the sailors' fable, a gull trades her wings to a fish for a coat of silver scales — and spends the rest of the tale sinking slowly, wishing back what she gave away.
No one who tells it thinks a gull ever made such a bargain, and that is the point.

A fable does not ask to be believed: it is invention worn openly, animals doing impossible things so that the lesson underneath — what you surrender to become what you envy — can be handed over without an argument.

Fable is a genre label first — Aesop's talking foxes — but English also uses it dismissively, for any account that is invention wearing the clothes of fact: 'the numbers in the prospectus were pure fable.' Its neighbors divide the storytelling work: a parable keeps to lifelike, everyday people; a legend attaches itself to a real name or place and grows in the telling; a myth expands to explain a people's whole world.
In this unit's spirit, remember the dismissive sense — calling a report a fable is a polite way of calling it false.

Every schoolchild knows the fable: the ant works all summer, the grasshopper fiddles, and winter settles the argument.
The entomologist Elena Ruiz has spent a career being mildly annoyed by it.
Real grasshoppers, she points out, do not starve for laziness — most species simply die before winter, industrious or not, and no amount of summer prudence would save them.
But she concedes the story was never about insects.
Its talking idlers and smug workers exist to hand children a lesson about planning, and the entomology is beside the point.
That, she tells her students, is the bargain such tales make: they lie freely about the world in order to say one true thing about us.
